r: The applied work here is comparative institutional analysis: describing how self-pay, private, and government-subsidized systems differ across industrialized and developing nations, and explaining how economic, political, cultural, and technological context shapes delivery and management. These are desk-research and synthesis tasks, mapping to Getting Information and Interpreting the Meaning of Information for Others, and task-exposure research finds writing and synthesis work positively associated with exposure, while observed-usage data shows this kind of analytical writing is already common in current AI use. No clinical embodiment or licensure caps the course, but it carries a Social and Behavioral Sciences plus Global Diversity general-studies designation, a state transfer-core mandate that requires some course fulfilling this slot rather than this specific one. At 24 months, adoption of AI research tools remains uneven across instructors and programs, so the realized rating is Low despite clear underlying capability.

By 2031, AI systems will competently draft comparative health-system analyses, pull cross-national policy data, and synthesize historical and cultural context, tasks squarely inside the writing-and-research category that observed-usage data shows dominating current AI use. The instrumental case for a student to build this synthesis skill by hand erodes substantially, since nothing about global health-systems comparison sits outside AI's digital, text-based competence. What holds the rating down is not task difficulty but the general-studies designation: the gtPathways transfer-core structure requires some course meet this Social and Behavioral Sciences and Global Diversity slot, not this exact course, so the institutional cap constrains the rating even as capability climbs. The result is Medium rather than High. Confidence in the direction is reasonable, though which comparative-analysis skills instructors still require students to demonstrate by hand is harder to predict.

A decade out, the central case has AI performing the great majority of comparative health-policy research and synthesis this course teaches, drafting cross-national analyses that once took students substantial library and library-database work to produce. The underlying task exposure argues for a high rating, consistent with task-exposure research's finding that writing-heavy synthesis work is strongly exposed. But the general-studies designation is a statutory, slow-moving structure, and the gtPathways requirement that some course fill this transfer slot persists regardless of any one course's content, holding the rating at Medium rather than tracking the raw capability curve. Ten-year capability forecasts carry real uncertainty, per METR/Epoch trend extrapolation, and how curricula respond to that capability is even less predictable than the capability itself; no confident point-prediction is warranted, but institutional lock-in is the more durable constraint here than task difficulty.
HCM 2010.d: In this course, students will analyze the structure of healthcare systems, whether self-pay, privately funded or government-subsidized in industrialized and developing nations. Emphasis is placed on the similarities and differences, as well as the context of economic, historical/political, social/cultural, and technological frameworks of healthcare systems. The global interdependence among nations and economies has an effect on the delivery and management of healthcare services around the world.

r: The course builds research, APA writing, scholarly-source evaluation, professional communication, and project-management skills that prepare students for their senior experience, mapping to Documenting/Recording Information and Organizing, Planning, and Prioritizing Work. These are writing-and-research tasks that task-exposure research classifies as positively associated with AI exposure, and observed-usage data shows writing and office-productivity tasks are already a leading category of model use. There is no licensure lock or clinical embodiment here; this is a general professional-skills course. What partially protects it at 24 months is its scaffolding role: it explicitly prepares students for the senior experience and later coursework, so even though AI competently drafts citations and outlines, the course's function of building durable research habits keeps the instrumental need only partially eroded, yielding Medium rather than a higher rating.

By 2031, AI writing assistants will competently handle APA formatting, source evaluation summaries, and cover-letter or resume drafting, the mechanical core of what this course currently teaches by hand. Productivity research on professional writing tasks already shows large time savings alongside quality gains when AI assists drafting, and that pattern plausibly extends to the research-and-professional-communication tasks this course covers. The scaffolding role that held the rating at Medium wanes at this horizon, since the course's foundational cap only binds strongly in the near term; by five years the underlying task exposure dominates. No accreditation or licensure structure protects this course, and its content is fully digital. The result is High, with moderate confidence, since exactly how AI literacy gets folded into a first-year-experience course rather than replacing it is a judgment call.

A decade out, the central case has AI performing most of the mechanical research-and-writing work this course teaches, drafting literature summaries, structuring project plans, and producing professional documents competently on request. The course's original scaffolding function, preparing students for a senior capstone, likely persists in some form, but the specific skills it drills, manual citation management, source triage, document formatting, are exactly the kind of exposed, non-foundational tasks that erode fastest under sustained capability growth. Task-exposure research's finding that writing skills are strongly positively associated with exposure argues for a high rating, and no institutional lock offsets that. The honest hedge is that ten-year predictions about how introductory professional-skills curricula get redesigned around AI tools are inherently uncertain; the rating is High, but with real uncertainty about the surviving pedagogical core.
HCM 2500.d: In this course, students prepare for the healthcare field and their senior experience by developing essential skills in research, communication, and professional conduct. Students explore senior experience requirements, plan for academic and career goals, and investigate diverse healthcare careers. The course content emphasizes ethical standards, effective teamwork, and proficient use of software applications important when working in the healthcare field. Students develop advanced writing skills using APA guidelines, conduct critical evaluations of scholarly sources, and apply project management and life skills to real-world challenges in health care.

r: This course applies legal and ethical frameworks to health-care management: medical negligence and malpractice liability, records and information management, patient consent and confidentiality, contracts, and labor relations, mapping to Interpreting the Meaning of Information for Others and Evaluating Information to Determine Compliance with Standards. Legal-document analysis and compliance summarization are text-based tasks that task-exposure research associates positively with exposure, and current AI tools already draft plausible legal analyses. The binding constraint is verification burden: malpractice, consent, and confidentiality errors carry high cost and non-obvious failure modes, exactly the jagged-frontier condition where unsupervised AI users are measurably less accurate outside their expertise. At 24 months that dampens the rating despite clear underlying task exposure, and diffusion of AI legal-compliance tools into health-care administration remains partial. Rating Low, driven down from a Medium base by verification demands.

By 2031, AI legal-research and compliance-drafting tools will competently summarize case law, flag contractual risk, and draft privacy and consent documentation, absorbing much of the analytical work this course currently has students perform manually. Task-exposure research's classification of legal-adjacent writing and analysis as positively exposed supports a higher base rating at this horizon. What continues to dampen the rating is verification burden: malpractice and confidentiality determinations carry high error cost, and the jagged-frontier finding that AI users misjudge reliability outside a tool's actual competence is directly applicable to health-care legal compliance, where a confidently wrong reading of consent law is costly. No accreditation or foundational-scaffolding constraint applies. The rating is Medium, reflecting substantial erosion of the drafting and research work paired with a persistent, if narrowing, human-verification role.

A decade out, the central case has AI performing most routine health-care compliance research and documentation, drafting policy language, flagging contractual risk, and summarizing regulatory change, while human judgment concentrates on ambiguous liability questions and negotiated outcomes. The verification-burden dampener persists structurally, since malpractice and confidentiality failures remain high-cost and often non-obvious regardless of how capable the underlying model becomes, which is why the rating does not track the raw task-exposure curve up to High. Ten-year capability forecasts carry genuine uncertainty per METR-style extrapolation, and how health-care legal-compliance practice reorganizes around AI tools is harder still to predict. The rating is Medium, hedged: the drafting and research substrate is substantially automatable, but the course's core value, judgment under legal and ethical ambiguity, is the kind of low-verification-tolerance work that erosion reaches last.
HCM 3030.d: This course examines the legal and ethical issues involved in the management and delivery of health care services. Emphasis is placed on law as it pertains to medical negligence, malpractice/ professional liability, medical records/information management, patient consent, confidentiality/privacy, patient rights/responsibilities, contracts, labor relations, and other current issues.

r: This introductory course has students identify a health-and-wellness venture idea, apply entrepreneurial models and tools, draft a business plan, and pursue funding, mapping to Developing Objectives and Strategies and Thinking Creatively. Business-plan drafting, market framing, and funding-pitch writing are exactly the writing-and-planning tasks that observed-usage data shows are already a prominent share of current AI use, and task-exposure research classifies this kind of document-production work as positively associated with exposure. There is no licensure or accreditation lock on a one-credit elective course, and no embodiment constrains it; the work is entirely digital drafting and analysis. At 24 months, AI already competently drafts business-plan sections and funding narratives, so realized adoption is high even for student-level work. Rating High, reflecting both immediate capability and low institutional friction.

By 2031, AI tools will competently generate full business-plan drafts, market analyses, and funding pitches tailored to health-care ventures, the core deliverables this course currently has students produce by hand. Productivity research on professional writing already shows substantial time savings paired with quality improvements when AI assists document drafting, a pattern that extends naturally to venture planning. No accreditation floor, licensure requirement, or foundational-scaffolding role protects this elective course, and its content remains fully digital and text-based. The instrumental case for personally drafting a business plan from scratch, rather than directing and evaluating an AI-generated one, continues to weaken. The rating stays High, with moderate confidence, since course content this specific and low-stakes could just as easily be redesigned to teach AI-assisted venture ideation rather than eliminated outright.

A decade out, the central case has AI performing the substantial majority of business-plan drafting, market analysis, and funding-narrative work this course teaches, competently and on demand. Nothing structural protects this course from that erosion: it carries no accreditation or licensure lock, sits outside any required sequence, and its subject matter, venture ideation and plan-writing, is squarely inside the digital, low-verification-burden zone where task-exposure research finds the strongest positive association. The honest hedge concerns pedagogy rather than capability: ten years is long enough that a course like this could be reframed around AI-augmented entrepreneurship rather than disappearing, and predicting that curricular choice with confidence is not warranted. On the narrow question of whether the instrumental need to manually produce these documents persists, the rating is High.
HCM 3100.d: This course serves as an introduction to entrepreneurism in health and wellness. Topics addressed in the class include: becoming an entrepreneur and finding a worthwhile project, the models and tools that entrepreneurs use, leveraging available resources, unique challenges in health care, creating a business plan, and attracting funding. Best practices will be examined and techniques applied through the use of real world examples of innovation in health care.

r: This course orients students broadly to health-care organizational structure and management practice: the interplay of cultural, economic, political, technological, and social forces in delivery, how health-care management differs from other professional management, ethical patient-care considerations, and disease origins and epidemiology as management background, mapping to Coordinating the Work and Activities of Others and Getting Information. The management and organizational-analysis portions are exposed, consistent with observed-usage data's dominant Computer and Mathematical category, but the epidemiology background component leans toward science content that task-exposure research finds negatively associated with exposure. More decisive is this course's role as the gateway prerequisite for human resources, leadership, and health-information-systems coursework in the program; that foundational-scaffolding function caps the rating regardless of task exposure. Rating Medium, driven by the prerequisite-substrate constraint rather than by task difficulty.

By 2031, AI will competently handle much of the descriptive and analytical content this survey course covers, summarizing organizational structures, explaining regulatory and cultural context, and drafting epidemiological background, tasks that skew toward the exposed end given the course's administrative framing. Left unconstrained, the underlying capability trajectory would push this rating toward High. But this course is the explicit prerequisite for at least three other required upper-division HCM courses in the program, a critical-substrate role that the deterministic framework caps at Medium regardless of how automatable the surface content becomes, because the course's function is building a durable conceptual base subsequent coursework depends on. The rating holds at Medium. Confidence in the foundational role is high, given explicit prerequisite listings; confidence in exactly how fast the surface content automates is more moderate.

A decade out, AI plausibly performs most of the descriptive organizational-analysis and background-research work this survey course currently assigns, consistent with sustained capability growth per METR-style trend extrapolation. Yet the course's structural role as the program's gateway prerequisite does not weaken with capability; if anything, a foundational course that other required coursework depends on is the kind of scaffolding that curricula are slowest to restructure, since doing so requires resequencing the entire major rather than one course. That keeps the rating capped at Medium even under an aggressive capability read. The genuine uncertainty is whether the program eventually redesigns its gateway course around AI-native management analysis; that curricular question is harder to forecast than the task capability itself. The rating is Medium, anchored by prerequisite lock-in rather than by task difficulty.
HCM 3150.d: Students in the course become familiar with the organizational structure of the health care field and are provided a general orientation to management practices within the industry. Emphasis is placed on the inter-relatedness of cultural, economic, political, technological and social aspects of health care delivery, along with its services and management. Further, the course content emphasizes the differences in management of health care from other professional areas and the importance of patient care and ethical issues for the manager to consider. Disease origins and epidemiology are explored as background for the aspiring management student.

r: This course introduces quality-assurance methods and tools across hospitals, ambulatory care, managed care, and public health: utilization review, continuous quality improvement, and total quality management, mapping to Analyzing Data or Information and Evaluating Information to Determine Compliance with Standards. The applied work, building dashboards, running utilization analyses, and documenting CQI processes, is analytical and reporting-heavy, squarely inside the Computer and Mathematical category that observed-usage data identifies as the largest current AI-use category. There is no clinical embodiment or licensure lock on this administrative course, only partial institutional grounding in a regulated health-care setting. At 24 months, AI competently supports quality analytics and report drafting, but near-term diffusion into health-care quality departments remains uneven and the regulated context sustains some near-term human involvement. Rating Medium, reflecting exposed tasks tempered by adoption timing and sector oversight.

By 2031, AI will plausibly perform much of the analytical and reporting core of health-care quality management, building utilization dashboards, running CQI trend analysis, and drafting compliance documentation, work that task-exposure research classifies as positively exposed and that observed-usage data already shows concentrated in the Computer and Mathematical category. The course's partial institutional grounding, contributing to but not independently mandating a licensure or accreditation credit floor, does not rise to a binding lock at this horizon. The residual is oversight judgment in a regulated, consequential setting: verifying that AI-generated utilization findings are sound before they inform patient-care decisions. That residual is real but narrower than the course's full methods content. Rating High: the applied quality-management work is substantially automatable, with the health-care governance context sustaining a meaningful but shrinking human-verification role.

A decade out, the central case has AI performing most routine health-care quality analytics and CQI documentation, with human involvement concentrated in governance, accountability, and judgment calls the regulatory environment requires rather than in producing the analysis itself. The instrumental case for a course teaching quality-management methods is substantially eroded at this horizon, since the underlying tasks are digital, non-embodied, and only partially institutionally grounded. The rating is High, hedged by the possibility that health-care's liability and regulatory structure sustains more human involvement in quality functions than a pure capability read would suggest, and by the general uncertainty attached to any ten-year capability forecast. The administrative, non-clinical character of this course, distinct from clinical-adjacent HCM content, is precisely why it tracks the exposed end of the catalog rather than the protected end.
HCM 3200.d: This course is an introduction to the methods and tools for managing quality in health care, and developments in quality assurance, utilization review, continuous quality improvement, and total quality management in health services, including hospitals, ambulatory care settings, managed care and public health.

r: This course covers health-care human-resource functions: competencies, structures, performance management, legal and labor issues, benefits, recruitment and retention, plus cover-letter, resume, and interview-technique practice from both applicant and manager perspectives, mapping to Staffing Organizational Units and Interviewing Applicants. Resume screening, policy drafting, and benefits administration are administrative tasks that observed-usage data and task-exposure research both associate positively with AI exposure, and applicant-tracking tools already perform much of this work commercially. The binding constraint is verification burden: labor and employment-law compliance carries real liability, and misapplied legal or labor guidance is a costly, non-obvious failure mode. That dampens the rating even though the underlying administrative tasks are highly exposed and adoption of AI-assisted HR tools in health-care settings is still uneven. Rating Low, pulled down by legal-compliance verification demands.

By 2031, AI HR tools will competently handle resume screening, benefits administration, performance-management documentation, and recruitment-workflow tasks, substantially eroding the administrative core this course currently teaches by hand; this tracks observed-usage data's finding that office and administrative tasks are heavily represented in current AI use. The employment-law and labor-relations component keeps a dampener in place, since compliance failures carry real liability and the jagged-frontier finding that AI users misjudge reliability outside a tool's competence is directly applicable to labor-law interpretation. No accreditation or foundational-scaffolding constraint applies beyond that verification concern. The rating is Medium: routine HR execution is substantially automatable, but legal and labor judgment sustains a persistent, narrower human role that keeps the course from tracking straight to High.

A decade out, AI plausibly performs the great majority of routine HR administration in health-care organizations, screening, benefits processing, performance documentation, and drafting recruitment materials, while human HR professionals concentrate on legal-compliance judgment, labor-relations negotiation, and organizational culture decisions. The verification-burden dampener persists structurally, since employment-law misapplication remains high-cost and non-obvious regardless of model capability, which is why the rating does not rise to High even under an aggressive capability read. Ten-year forecasts carry genuine uncertainty about how HR practice reorganizes around AI tools, and predicting the surviving scope of manager-level HR judgment with confidence is not warranted. The rating is Medium, reflecting substantial erosion of administrative execution paired with a durable, if narrower, legal and labor-judgment core the course still serves.
HCM 3400.d: This course is designed to analyze principles significant to human resource management in health care. Specific attention is placed on human resource functions, competencies, structures, quality, performance management, legal and labor issues, benefits, and recruitment and retention. Students explore the development of cover letters, resumes, and different interview techniques from both applicant and manager perspectives.

r: This course teaches the research process, research terminology, and the use of research to improve health-care financing, delivery, and management, with students critiquing published research articles, identifying funding sources, and applying findings to management projects, mapping to Evaluating Information to Determine Compliance with Standards and Updating and Using Relevant Knowledge. Critiquing research quality and methodology is a critical-thinking task that task-exposure research finds strongly negatively associated with AI exposure, distinguishing it from routine writing or summarization work. AI tools can already draft literature summaries, but assessing whether a study's methodology supports its management conclusions is a judgment task with high error cost if delegated uncritically. That verification burden dampens the rating at 24 months alongside modest realized capability for research-quality assessment specifically. Rating Low, protected primarily by the critical-evaluation core of the course.

By 2031, AI research-assistant tools will competently locate literature, summarize findings, and draft funding-source overviews, absorbing the retrieval-and-synthesis portion of this course's content, consistent with observed-usage data showing research-synthesis tasks are a growing share of AI use. What continues to protect the rating is the course's core skill: critically evaluating whether a study's methodology and evidence actually support the management conclusions drawn from it. Task-exposure research's finding that critical-thinking skills are negatively associated with exposure applies directly here, and the jagged-frontier evidence, that AI users are measurably less accurate outside a tool's real competence, is a live risk when research-quality judgment is delegated to a model that cannot reliably assess its own evidentiary limits. Rating stays Low, reflecting a course whose distinguishing skill is the harder-to-automate half of research work.

A decade out, AI research tools will plausibly perform most literature retrieval, summarization, and funding-landscape mapping competently, and the instrumental case for teaching those mechanical skills by hand continues to erode. But the course's central pedagogical function, teaching students to critically evaluate research quality and apply findings responsibly to management decisions, is precisely the critical-thinking work that task-exposure research identifies as most resistant to AI substitution, and the verification burden of trusting an AI's own quality assessment of research remains real even under substantial capability growth. That shifts the rating to Medium at this horizon, reflecting erosion of the retrieval-and-summary tasks while the evaluative core persists. Ten-year capability trajectories carry genuine uncertainty, and whether AI eventually handles methodological critique reliably enough to remove this dampener is not confidently predictable.
HCM 3500.d: This course examines the research process, research terminology and the role of research as a tool for understanding and improving financing, delivery, and management in health care organizations. Students critique relevant research articles, explore sources of funding for research projects, and apply this knowledge to health care management projects.

r: This course covers leadership traits, styles, and skills in health care, the tools leaders use, leading through crises, and leading multicultural teams, with students examining their own leadership traits and analyzing others' styles, mapping to Guiding, Directing, and Motivating Subordinates and Resolving Conflicts and Negotiating with Others. Crisis leadership and real-time team direction are interpersonal, presence-dependent activities that task-exposure research and observed-usage data both place at the low end of AI exposure, distinct from document-based management writing. Judgment errors in crisis leadership carry high, sometimes non-obvious cost, which further limits how much AI output a manager could safely rely on unverified. Neither factor alone would fully protect the course, but together, low embodiment score and low verification tolerance, they dampen the rating even from an already-modest base. Rating Low at 24 months.

By 2031, AI tools will plausibly help leaders analyze team dynamics or draft crisis-communication plans, but the core competence this course builds, real-time interpersonal leadership under pressure, motivating subordinates, negotiating conflict, adapting to a multicultural team in the room, remains categorically different from a task an AI performs on the leader's behalf. Task-exposure research's low-exposure classification for presence-based, real-time interpersonal work applies directly, and the jagged-frontier finding about misplaced trust in AI outputs is a live concern precisely in crisis situations where verification time is scarcest. Both the embodiment and verification-burden factors keep dampening what capability growth alone would otherwise raise. The rating holds at Low. Confidence is moderate given this course's brief, generalist description, but the fundamentally interpersonal nature of its content is unambiguous.

A decade out, AI will likely be embedded in the tools health-care leaders use for team analytics, scheduling, and crisis-communication drafting, but the instrumental question this framework asks, whether AI performs the work this course's knowledge is applied to, keeps returning a low answer, because that work is leading real people through real crises in real time. Neither the embodiment-and-presence factor nor the verification-burden factor is capability-dependent in the way document-based analytical courses are; leadership judgment under pressure with a multicultural team is not delegable regardless of how far model capability advances. The honest uncertainty concerns which supporting tools leaders will use, not whether the leadership competence itself remains necessary. Rating stays Low, anchored by durable embodiment and verification-burden protections rather than by any confident capability ceiling.
HCM 3550.d: This course is an introduction to the concepts of leadership in health care. It presents the traits, styles and skills of effective leaders. It also addresses the tools and techniques used by leaders within health care organizations. Leadership during crises and of multicultural teams is analyzed. Students gain understanding of personal leadership traits and examine others' leadership styles.

r: This course introduces health-care management information systems: the role of electronic communication and data transmission, planning and change management for health-IT adoption, and patient-centered technologies in the modern health enterprise, mapping to Interacting With Computers and Analyzing Data or Information. This content sits squarely in the Computer and Mathematical domain that observed-usage data identifies as the largest current category of AI use, and task-exposure research finds programming- and technology-adjacent work strongly positively associated with exposure. AI already competently explains health-IT system architecture, drafts change-management plans, and summarizes data-transmission standards. There is no embodiment or licensure constraint on this administrative, conceptual course, and no accreditation credit-hour floor is documented. At 24 months, realized capability for this kind of technology-planning content is already substantial. Rating High, reflecting both strong task exposure and the absence of protective constraints.

By 2031, AI will competently perform much of the health-IT planning, systems documentation, and change-management drafting this course teaches, consistent with the METR/Epoch capability trend of rapidly expanding task-time horizons for digital, information-processing work. The course's content, understanding and planning around information systems rather than performing clinical care, has no embodiment constraint and no accreditation or licensure lock to cap the rating. Verification burden is moderate rather than severe, since health-IT planning decisions are consequential but not immediately safety-critical in the way clinical judgment is, so no dampener applies. The instrumental case for a student to learn this content primarily to perform the planning work personally, rather than to direct and evaluate AI-assisted systems, continues to weaken. Rating High, with moderate confidence given the general, introductory framing of the course description.

A decade out, the central case has AI performing the substantial majority of health-information-systems planning, documentation, and change-management drafting that this introductory course covers, extending the trajectory already visible in the Computer and Mathematical usage category. No structural protection, no embodiment, no licensure, no foundational-scaffolding role beyond a single prerequisite, holds the rating down, and ten-year capability extrapolation per METR/Epoch-style trend reasoning continues to favor strong exposure for digital systems-planning content specifically. The genuine uncertainty is less about whether the underlying tasks automate and more about how health-IT governance and patient-data oversight roles get reorganized around AI-managed systems, a structural, organizational question current evidence does not resolve with confidence, unlike the more predictable trajectory of the planning and documentation tasks themselves. On the narrower instrumental question this framework asks, the rating is High, held with only moderate confidence given the course's brief description.
HCM 3600.d: This course is a general introduction to health care management information system, focusing on the role and importance of electronic communication and data transmission. Planning and change management in health care information technology are emphasized. The materials cover patient-centered technologies found in the health enterprise today.

r: The course examines health disparities across racial and ethnic groups, applying public health and healthcare management theory to connect health data patterns to individual, community, policy, and system-level outcomes. The applied tasks are interpreting disaggregated data, weighing structural causes, and drafting equity-oriented recommendations, which sit closer to the critical-thinking end of the spectrum that task-exposure research finds negatively associated with automation exposure, unlike routine reporting. AI already drafts competent disparities narratives and summarizes literature, but assigning causal weight to social determinants and recommending policy responses is consequential if a model launders bias from training data, and such errors are not obvious to an unprepared reader. That verification burden anchors the rating at 24 months even as underlying data-analysis tasks grow AI-assisted; no accreditation or licensure mandate locks the course institutionally, so the rating tracks exposure and oversight need directly.

By 2031, AI tools will competently synthesize health-disparities datasets, draft comparative analyses across demographic groups, and produce first-pass policy memos, meaningfully eroding the instrumental case for a student to build these analytical skills from scratch. Observed-usage data already shows writing and office-analysis tasks concentrated among the most common AI use cases, and that pattern should deepen. What keeps the rating at Medium rather than higher is the persistent verification burden: equity analysis is exactly the domain where the jagged-frontier finding applies, since AI users working outside a model's reliable competence show materially lower accuracy while trusting the output more, and disparities work touches politically and ethically sensitive judgments about causation and remedy. No institutional lock offsets this. The course's value increasingly shifts toward teaching students to catch subtle misattributions in AI-generated equity analysis rather than to produce the analysis unaided.

A decade out, AI should handle most of the descriptive and comparative work of health-disparities analysis — pulling data, identifying gaps, generating draft narratives — with reasonable competence, consistent with the fast capability trajectory documented in task-time-horizon research. The instrumental case for teaching students to perform this analysis manually weakens further. The rating stays Medium rather than rising to High because the course's core content — attributing disparities to structural causes and recommending equitable interventions — remains judgment-laden, ethically loaded work where science and critical-thinking skills are the categories task-exposure research most consistently protects, and where mis-specified AI reasoning about causation carries real policy consequences. Ten-year forecasts carry real uncertainty about whether verification tooling matures enough to close that gap; absent stronger evidence the course is rated as still requiring a human who understands the underlying disparities frameworks, not merely one who can prompt a model.
HCM 3700.d: Students in this course engage in a comprehensive exploration and identification of key concepts related to diversity, inclusion, and health disparities. Students examine health data across racial and ethnic groups and using grounded public health and healthcare management theories to analyze the impact of health disparities on individuals, communities, policies, and national systems. Through this course, students develop a nuanced understanding of how health disparities are influenced by various factors and gain practical skills to contribute to more equitable healthcare solutions.

r: This one-credit orientation course covers basic practice-management concepts, skills, and functions for running a healthcare professional practice — scheduling logic, staffing coordination, and administrative workflow fundamentals. These are generic office-management tasks rather than clinically embodied or highly specialized ones, and they map closely to the administrative and writing activities that observed-usage data already shows concentrated among common AI applications. At 24 months, AI tools competently draft policies, staffing templates, and operational checklists of the kind this course introduces, partially eroding the instrumental need to learn them from a dedicated course. The rating holds at Medium rather than higher because deployment inside small healthcare practices still lags broader diffusion trends, and the course's brief, generic description limits how confidently its specific tasks can be pinned to fully mature AI workflows this early.

By 2031, general practice-management functions — scheduling frameworks, basic staffing and budget templates, standard operating procedures — should be substantially automatable, consistent with productivity research showing large speed and quality gains on structured professional writing and administrative tasks, with the biggest uplift for less experienced practitioners. Because this is a broad orientation course with no embodied or clinically supervised component and no accreditation-specific mandate tying it to a required credit floor, nothing structurally protects it from that erosion. The rating rises to High: the instrumental case for a dedicated course teaching generic practice-management orientation weakens substantially once AI can generate and adapt these materials on demand. Some hedge remains because the course's actual assessed tasks are underspecified, and administrative competence in a live healthcare office still involves judgment AI drafting tools do not fully replace.

Ten years out, the basic administrative and planning functions this orientation course introduces are very plausibly default AI-assisted work in most healthcare practices, following the fast capability trajectory documented in task-time-horizon research and continuing diffusion of office-automation tools into small-practice settings. The rating remains High, reflecting that this is thin, generic administrative content with no institutional or embodiment anchor to resist erosion. The central uncertainty is less about capability, which is likely sufficient well before 2036, and more about whether healthcare practices — often small, resource-constrained organizations — have actually adopted such tools by then, since diffusion research shows capability consistently outruns real-world uptake. The course's brief, low-specificity description also limits how precisely its particular skills can be mapped to displaced tasks, which is reflected in the confidence rating rather than the exposure judgment itself.
HCM 3750.d: This course is designed to provide a general orientation to practice management in the field of health care. The focus is on basic practice management concepts, skills, and functions considered necessary for effective and successful healthcare professional practice management.

r: The course teaches analytic techniques for a data-driven healthcare industry — spreadsheeting, formulating study questions, report writing, and presentations — applied to measuring health system performance, comparing delivery models, and assessing population health. These tasks map directly onto the Computer & Mathematical category that observed-usage data identifies as the largest single category of AI use, and spreadsheet and report-drafting work of this kind is already competently AI-assisted. At 24 months, that yields real but partial erosion: AI can produce first-pass analyses and slide decks, but formulating the right study questions and validating that health-system performance comparisons are methodologically sound still needs a person who understands the underlying data. No accreditation or clinical mandate protects the course, so the Medium rating reflects genuine current exposure rather than institutional insulation.

By 2031, AI systems should competently execute most of the spreadsheeting, comparative analysis, and presentation-building this course teaches, in line with real-deliverable benchmarks showing frontier models approaching, though not yet matching, human-expert quality on occupational analytical work, and with documented large speed gains on structured technical tasks. Because the course has no embodied component, no licensure gate, and no accreditation credit-hour floor, capability growth translates fairly directly into instrumental erosion. The rating rises to High: a student can increasingly generate competent health-system performance comparisons and population-health assessments with AI assistance rather than needing the course's manual-technique training. The hedge is that formulating well-posed study questions — the course's stated first skill — remains a genuinely difficult prompt-engineering-adjacent task where quality still depends on domain understanding AI does not supply on its own.

A decade out, the descriptive and comparative analytics this course teaches are plausibly near-fully automatable, consistent with the rapid task-time-horizon doubling documented in capability research, and the instrumental rationale for teaching manual spreadsheeting and report-building techniques is substantially weakened. The rating stays High. The genuine uncertainty at this horizon is less about whether AI can execute the mechanics — that seems likely — and more about whether health systems' data governance and adoption pace keep up, since diffusion research consistently shows real-world uptake lagging raw capability by years. There is no institutional floor here to slow that erosion regardless of adoption pace, so the ten-year hedge is calibrated to capability and deployment uncertainty rather than to any structural protection for the course's content.
HCM 3830.d: This course allows the student to explore the role of analytics in supporting a complex, data-driven, healthcare industry. Key topics include analytic techniques and methods (spreadsheeting, formulating study questions, report writing, presentations) to examine issues such as measuring health system performance, comparing health care delivery, and assessing the health of populations.

r: This course builds a foundation in descriptive and inferential statistics for healthcare data using analytical software such as SAS, covering the mechanics of running and interpreting statistical procedures on health datasets. Task-exposure research explicitly names quantitative analysts among the most-exposed occupational categories, and statistical-software workflows are a natural fit for current AI code-generation and interpretation capabilities. At 24 months, AI tools can already draft and explain statistical syntax and summarize output competently for standard procedures, partially eroding the case for manual instruction in the mechanics. The rating holds at Medium rather than higher because correctly selecting a statistical test for a given health-data design and catching violated assumptions still benefits from a human who understands inferential logic, not just software syntax, and near-term healthcare-sector adoption of such tools remains uneven.

By 2031, AI assistance for statistical-software workflows should be well-established, competently generating code, running standard inferential procedures, and explaining results in plain language, consistent with the strong association task-exposure research finds between programming-adjacent tasks and automation exposure. With no licensure gate, accreditation floor, or embodied component protecting this course, that capability growth converts into a High rating: the instrumental need to learn SAS-style statistical mechanics by hand diminishes as AI increasingly handles both the coding and the first-pass interpretation. The hedge is that health datasets often carry design complications — missing data, confounding, small subpopulations — where the jagged-frontier finding applies directly: AI users working outside reliable competence show materially worse accuracy while trusting outputs more, so some statistical judgment remains genuinely load-bearing.

Ten years out, statistical analysis of health data is plausibly executed largely by AI end to end — from procedure selection through output interpretation — given the fast task-time-horizon growth documented in capability research and the already-strong exposure of quantitative-analyst work identified in task-exposure studies. The rating remains High. What keeps this from certainty is the difficulty of statistical reasoning under real-world health-data messiness, where subtle misapplications are exactly the non-obvious failure mode the verification-burden concept describes, and where healthcare organizations may be slower than average to trust fully automated inferential pipelines given liability concerns and cautious adoption patterns. No institutional floor offsets this exposure regardless, so the ten-year hedge reflects capability and adoption uncertainty rather than any structural protection built into the course's accreditation status or curricular placement.
HCM 3840.d: This course will provide students with a general foundation of descriptive and inferential statistics of health care data using an analytical statistical software application, eg, SAS or similar application.

r: As the capstone experience of the Health Data Science Certificate, this course covers health data sets as they scope business and clinical intelligence, applying data-science and statistical tooling alongside data quality and governance concepts. Database schema work, query writing, and data-quality documentation are close analogs to software and data-engineering tasks where AI code-assistance tools already show large measured speed gains. At 24 months this yields Medium exposure: AI competently drafts queries and flags data-quality issues, but designing governance frameworks for sensitive health data and judging what is fit for clinical or business intelligence use still needs someone who understands both the technical schema and the healthcare-specific stakes. No accreditation mandate protects the course, so the rating tracks the underlying task mix directly rather than any institutional floor.

By 2031, AI coding assistants should handle most routine database administration and query-writing tasks competently, building on productivity research already showing very large task-speed gains for AI-assisted software work, and data-quality checks should be substantially automatable as well. With no licensure gate or credit-hour mandate anchoring this course and no embodied component, that capability growth converts fairly directly into a High rating: the instrumental case for hand-building database administration skills for health data weakens as AI increasingly performs the schema design and governance documentation the course teaches. The hedge is that emerging trends in health data governance move quickly and unevenly across organizations, and the course's own description of a fast-changing landscape suggests continued need for someone who can adapt AI-generated database work to shifting compliance requirements.

A decade out, database administration and data-governance documentation for health data are plausibly default AI-assisted tasks, consistent with the rapid capability growth documented in task-time-horizon research, and the instrumental rationale for a dedicated course teaching these mechanics by hand is substantially eroded. The rating stays High. As the certificate's terminal course rather than a prerequisite substrate for further coursework, nothing about its position in the curriculum protects it either. The genuine uncertainty is around adoption pace inside healthcare organizations, which diffusion research shows lagging capability broadly across sectors, and around whether health-data governance requirements grow more rather than less complex over the decade, which could sustain more human oversight of AI-generated database and compliance work than a pure capability read implies at present.
HCM 3850.d: This course will provide students with the tools to understand the role of health data sets in defining and scoping business and clinical intelligence and apply the techniques of data science and statistical tools. This course provides an overview of data quality and governance, specific issues in various types of health care analyses, and emerging trends, and offers a final experience in the Health Data Science Certificate Program.

r: This course, the certificate's final experience alongside HCM 3850, applies data-science and statistical tools to scope business and clinical intelligence from health data sets, with attention to data quality, governance, and emerging analytic trends. Business-intelligence work — building dashboards, summarizing performance metrics, drafting interpretive narratives for decision-makers — sits squarely in the Computer & Mathematical usage category that observed-usage data identifies as the largest current AI application area. At 24 months, AI already drafts competent BI summaries and visualizations, giving partial erosion of the instrumental case; what a person still needs to supply is judgment about which metrics matter for a specific healthcare organization's decisions and whether governance constraints are being respected. No accreditation lock offsets that exposure, so the Medium rating tracks the task mix rather than institutional protection.

By 2031, AI tools should competently generate business-intelligence dashboards, performance narratives, and comparative reporting for healthcare organizations, consistent with real-deliverable benchmarks showing frontier models closing in on human-expert quality on occupational analytical output. With no licensure or accreditation floor and no embodied component, that capability shift converts to a High rating: the instrumental need to hand-build BI reporting and interpretation skills weakens as AI increasingly performs both the analysis and the decision-facing narrative the course teaches. The hedge is that translating BI output into sound organizational decisions in a regulated, high-stakes health-care context still carries real verification weight, and enterprise-context evidence shows AI assistance skews toward automating rather than merely augmenting this kind of analytical work, which cuts toward higher exposure but also higher consequences for unreviewed errors.

Ten years out, most of the mechanical work of health-care business intelligence — building dashboards, generating comparative analyses, drafting interpretive summaries — is plausibly AI-executed by default, following the fast capability trajectory in task-time-horizon research, and the instrumental case for a dedicated course teaching these techniques by hand is substantially eroded. The rating remains High. As a terminal, capstone-style course rather than a foundational prerequisite, its position in the curriculum offers no structural protection either. The lasting uncertainty concerns whether healthcare organizations' data governance and interpretive judgment requirements keep a human decision-maker meaningfully in the loop for translating BI output into policy and operational choices, since heavier regulation could sustain more oversight than a pure capability read of the analytic tasks alone would suggest.
HCM 3860.d: This course will provide students with the tools to understand the role of health data sets in defining and scoping business and clinical intelligence and apply the techniques of data science and statistical tools. This course provides an overview of data quality and governance, specific issues in various types of health care analyses, and emerging trends, and offers a final experience in the Health Data Science Certificate Program.

r: This is a supervised, faculty-mentored field placement in a real healthcare organization, arranged through the Classroom to Career Hub, where the applied work is whatever a specific department assigns — but the course's actual instrumental function is placing a student physically inside an organization to build supervised, accountable, real-time working relationships with staff and colleagues. That embodied, interpersonal placement is precisely the category task-exposure research identifies as low-exposure relative to programming and writing work. Even where discrete tasks the intern performs are digital and AI-assistable, the course's value lies in supervised on-site performance and relationship-building that cannot be replicated remotely by a model. At 24 months, no AI capability substitutes for physical presence and accountable, live workplace judgment, so the rating is Low regardless of how automatable individual sub-tasks become.

By 2031, AI tools will plausibly assist interns with drafting documents, summarizing meetings, and handling routine administrative sub-tasks during their placement, but the course's core instrumental function — supervised, embodied, real-time professional experience inside a health-care organization, with faculty oversight of performance the department requires before enrollment — is unaffected by that kind of augmentation. Verification burden also remains real: performance in a live organizational setting under professional and faculty accountability carries consequences that are not caught by a model check. Diffusion research shows AI adoption spreading unevenly and gradually across firms, and even where a host organization is AI-forward, the placement's value is the student's supervised presence in it, not the digital tasks performed inside it. The rating stays Low, hedged mainly by uncertainty over how internship task composition may shift.

A decade out, individual digital sub-tasks within an internship placement — drafting, scheduling, basic reporting — are very plausibly AI-assisted by default, but the course's instrumental purpose remains a supervised, embodied placement establishing real interpersonal professional relationships and accountable on-site performance in a health-care organization, arranged and monitored through a dedicated career-services process. That structure is not something an AI capability improvement displaces, since the requirement is physical and professional presence, not task throughput. The main uncertainty at ten years is whether the definition of what counts as valid hands-on experience evolves as remote and hybrid healthcare-administration work grows, which could loosen the embodiment requirement somewhat. Absent evidence of that shift, the rating stays Low, reflecting that this course is structurally different in kind from the analytical and business-knowledge courses in the same program.
HCM 3980.d: Supervised by a faculty member within the major department, internships provide practical, hands-on experience in a professional field related to the major. Internship placements must be established prior to enrollment in this course in consultation with the Classroom to Career (C2) Hub. Internship requirements vary by department. For information and instructions on finding and enrolling in an internship, contact the Classroom to Career (C2) Hub at [contact omitted].

r: The course covers fiscal analysis and control of health-care institutions — third-party payer and reimbursement issues, tax status, revenue, costs, charges, inventory and materials management, working capital, budgeting, and financial reporting. These are structured, quantitative, document-heavy tasks closely aligned with the Computer & Mathematical category observed-usage data identifies as the largest current AI application area, and financial-reporting drafting is already competently AI-assisted. At 24 months, AI can generate first-pass budget analyses and reimbursement calculations, partially eroding the instrumental case for learning the manual mechanics. The rating holds at Medium rather than higher because correctly interpreting payer-mix and reimbursement rules for a specific health-care institution still requires domain judgment, and no accreditation or licensure mandate protects the course, so the rating reflects genuine present-day exposure of the task set itself.

By 2031, AI tools should competently execute most of the structured financial-analysis and reporting tasks this course teaches, consistent with productivity research showing large time savings and quality gains on professional writing and analytical documentation, and with real-deliverable benchmarks showing frontier models closing in on expert-level output for occupational financial work. With no embodied component and no institutional lock, that capability growth converts to a High rating: the instrumental need to hand-build budgets, reimbursement analyses, and financial reports weakens substantially as AI increasingly performs both the calculation and the narrative reporting. The hedge is that health-care reimbursement rules are genuinely complex and change with policy, so verifying that an AI-generated financial analysis correctly reflects current payer requirements still carries real, non-trivial oversight weight.

Ten years out, most of the mechanical work of health-care financial management — budgeting, reimbursement calculation, financial reporting — is plausibly AI-executed by default, following the fast capability trajectory documented in task-time-horizon research, and the instrumental case for teaching these techniques manually is substantially eroded. The rating remains High. Because the course carries no accreditation-specific credit floor and no clinical or licensure gate, nothing structurally protects it from that erosion regardless of adoption pace. The genuine uncertainty concerns how much human financial oversight health-care institutions choose to retain given fiduciary and regulatory accountability for institutional finances, which could sustain more review of AI-generated financial work than a pure capability read suggests, and concerns general diffusion lag as health-care finance offices adopt these tools unevenly.
HCM 4030.d: This course surveys the organizational and operational aspects of fiscal analysis and control of health care institutions. Particular attention is given to the importance of third-party payer and reimbursement issues. Emphasis is placed on the practical processes involved in the determination and analysis of tax status, revenues, costs, charges, inventory/materials management, working capital levels, budgets, and financial reporting.

r: This course applies microeconomic theory to the health-care industry, examining how the delivery system functions within broad social, political, and economic contexts and analyzing public policy from an economic perspective. Applying economic theory to a specific, changing policy context is closer to the analytical-reasoning end of the spectrum that task-exposure research finds negatively associated with automation exposure than to routine data reporting, even though AI can already draft competent summaries of health-economics concepts. At 24 months, the risk that an AI-generated economic policy analysis misapplies theory to a specific institutional context — and that the error is not obvious to a reader without economics training — keeps verification burden high. That dampens what would otherwise be a Medium base rating down to Low; no accreditation mandate is doing the protective work here, the theoretical reasoning itself is.

By 2031, AI should competently draft health-economics analyses, summarize policy debates, and apply standard microeconomic frameworks to health-delivery questions, consistent with the broad task-exposure finding that writing-adjacent analytical output is increasingly automatable. That capability growth pushes the base rating to High. What holds the final rating at Medium is that applying economic theory correctly to a specific, evolving policy context remains exactly the kind of critical-thinking-protected work task-exposure research separates from routine tasks, and the jagged-frontier finding applies directly: users outside a model's reliable competence show meaningfully worse accuracy while trusting outputs more, which matters when the subject is health policy with real distributive consequences. Macro-level productivity effects from AI remain modest and slow per current estimates, reinforcing that the underlying economic environment this course analyzes is not itself being transformed quickly.

A decade out, AI likely handles most of the descriptive and comparative economic analysis this course teaches — summarizing market structures, modeling reimbursement effects, drafting policy briefs — with meaningful competence, given the rapid capability trajectory in task-time-horizon research. The rating stays Medium rather than rising further because correctly reasoning about how economic theory applies to a specific, shifting health-policy context remains judgment-laden work in a category task-exposure research consistently protects, and macro-level evidence suggests AI's aggregate economic effects remain modest even over multi-year horizons, implying the discipline's core analytical content is not being hollowed out as fast as pure task automation might suggest. Ten-year uncertainty is real: if verification tooling for economic reasoning matures substantially, this could shift toward High, but nothing in current evidence supports that as the central case yet.
HCM 4040.d: This course examines the major economic issues facing the health care industry with emphasis on microeconomic theory. The student assesses the relevance of economics to health and medical care and applies the principles to related health issues. The student will understand the mechanisms of the health care delivery system within the broad social, political, and economic contexts. The student will explore the ever changing nature of the health care industry and analyze related public policy from an economic perspective.

r: The course orients students to the structure and use of electronic medical records in supporting patient-care documentation, then applies database-administration and process-analysis skills to maintain and support an EMR application within a health-care organization. This is IT support and systems administration work — configuring, troubleshooting, and documenting a software application — not clinical care itself, and it maps closely to technical-support and database tasks where AI code and configuration assistance already shows measurable gains. At 24 months, AI competently assists with routine EMR configuration and documentation tasks, giving partial erosion; the rating holds at Medium rather than higher because EMR support work sits adjacent to patient-care documentation, where misconfiguration has downstream care consequences, keeping some verification burden intact even though the applied tasks themselves are fully digital and administrative in nature.

By 2031, AI tools should handle most routine database administration, configuration troubleshooting, and process-documentation tasks involved in EMR support, consistent with productivity research showing large measured speed gains for AI-assisted technical and software-support work. With no licensure gate protecting this specific administrative-support course and no embodied component, that capability growth converts to a High rating: the instrumental case for teaching manual database-administration and support techniques for EMR systems weakens as AI increasingly performs the configuration and process-analysis work directly. The hedge is that EMR systems sit at the center of patient-care documentation, so verifying that AI-assisted support changes have not introduced care-relevant errors remains a real, non-trivial check, and health-care IT environments have historically been slower than average to adopt new automation tooling given liability exposure.

Ten years out, EMR database administration, configuration, and process-support work is plausibly AI-executed by default, following the fast capability trajectory in task-time-horizon research and continuing diffusion of IT-automation tools into health-care organizations more broadly. The rating remains High. Nothing about the course's position in the curriculum or its accreditation status offers structural protection, since it is a support-and-administration course rather than a licensure-gated clinical one. The genuine uncertainty concerns how much human oversight health-care IT departments retain for systems this close to patient-care documentation, where regulatory and liability pressure could sustain more review of AI-configured EMR changes than a pure capability read implies, and concerns whether health-care organizations' historically cautious adoption pace for core clinical-adjacent systems holds unchanged over a full decade.
HCM 4150.d: Students in this course will be oriented to the detailed elements of an electronic medical record (EMR) and how it is used in the support of contemporary, patient-care services. The course will consist of several detailed experiential scenarios to familiarize the student with the use of the EMR in documenting patient-care services. The course will then lead the student through applying skills database administration and process analysis to maintain and support the EMR application in a health care organization.

r: HCM 4161 covers community risk assessment, NIMS/ICS planning, mutual-aid coordination, hazardous-materials and mass-casualty planning, and mitigation and recovery documentation. These map to Developing Objectives and Strategies and Documenting/Recording Information, where generative tools already draft plan templates, hazard-analysis narratives, and after-action reports. Task-exposure research classifies writing and planning content as strongly exposed, and observed-usage data shows Computer & Mathematical and office-writing categories dominating current adoption. Yet the course's real payoff is judgment under active incident-command conditions, coordinating multiple agencies while an emergency unfolds, where mistakes compound quickly and the verification burden stays meaningfully high. Diffusion data shows adoption remains uneven across public-sector emergency-management offices at this horizon. No licensure or accreditation floor protects the course, so its instrumental case rests on that unautomated coordination judgment rather than institutional lock-in, holding the 24-month rating at Low despite exposed planning-document tasks.

By 2031, AI drafting of emergency operations plans, hazard-mitigation narratives, and NIMS-compliant documentation will likely be routine, and utilization-review-style risk scoring will be common in emergency-management offices, consistent with the productivity literature's gains for structured writing tasks. The instrumental case for the documentation-heavy half of the course meaningfully erodes. What resists automation is live incident-command decision-making — allocating scarce resources across agencies during a mass-casualty or hazmat event — a real-time, high-consequence, interpersonal task the task-exposure literature places outside AI's frontier. Verification burden remains real: a mis-specified plan or misjudged incident-command call has non-obvious failure modes discovered only during an actual disaster. With no accreditation floor and only moderate foundational weight, the rating rises to Medium: planning content is broadly automatable while coordination judgment under duress is not, and the balance tips the course toward partial rather than full erosion.

A decade out, AI-assisted planning, simulation, and after-action analysis could handle most of the routine documentation this course teaches, and diffusion into public-sector emergency management should be considerably deeper than today's uneven adoption. The residual instrumental value concentrates in live incident-command judgment and multi-agency coordination during active disasters, a category task-exposure research continues to treat as resistant given its real-time, high-stakes, interpersonal character. Capability-trend evidence suggests systems capable of longer-horizon planning tasks by 2036, which could narrow this gap further than a central-case reading implies, but incident command during an unfolding hazmat or mass-casualty event is not a task organizations will delegate without a human anchor. Absent any licensure lock, the rating holds at Medium rather than climbing to High, reflecting genuine but bounded erosion and real ten-year uncertainty about how much coordination judgment eventually gets automated.
HCM 4161.d: Students examine concepts and principles of community risk assessment, planning, and response to fires, natural and man-made disasters, including National Institute Management System (NIMS) and Incident Command System (ICS), mutual aid and automatic response, training and preparedness, communications, civil disturbances, terrorist threats/incidents, hazardous materials planning, mass casualty incidents, earthquake preparedness, and disaster mitigation and recovery.

r: This course teaches the health care manager's role in strategic planning and the methodology of strategic management, emphasizing how organizations adapt to a changing environment. The applied work — environmental scanning, SWOT-style analysis, strategy-document drafting, and adaptation planning — maps to Developing Objectives and Strategies and Analyzing Data or Information, categories observed-usage data shows concentrated in the largest current adoption segment, Computer & Mathematical and office work. GDPval-style evaluation of real business deliverables shows models approaching but not yet matching expert strategy work, so competent drafts still need a manager's judgment before they are used. No licensure or accreditation floor constrains this administrative course, and it carries only moderate foundational weight in the curriculum. At 24 months AI already assists analysis and drafting meaningfully, moving the rating to Medium rather than leaving it at Low.

By 2031, AI tools should competently perform much of the analytical and drafting labor of health care strategic management — market and competitor analysis, scenario planning, strategy memos — consistent with productivity research showing large speed and quality gains on professional writing and analytical tasks. Enterprise data already show automation, rather than augmentation, dominating API usage in this kind of white-collar analytical work. The residual is executive judgment about which strategy to commit an organization to under real uncertainty, a narrower slice than the course's full methodology content. No embodiment, licensure, or accreditation constraint caps the rating, and the course's business-administrative character places it with other exposed management courses rather than protected clinical ones. The rating moves to High: the applied strategic-management work becomes largely AI-performable, with the manager's role narrowing toward final judgment and accountability.

A decade out, capability-trend evidence on lengthening AI task-time horizons suggests multi-step strategic analysis — the kind this course teaches through case methodology — sits well within reach, and macro-level diffusion, while still gradual by Acemoglu's estimate, should have progressed substantially in office-based industries like health administration by 2036. Most of the analytical and planning content the course delivers is plausibly AI-performable, leaving human health care managers concentrated on final strategic commitments, stakeholder accountability, and organizational politics that resist clean automation. No institutional lock-in exists to hold the rating down, and the course's terminal, non-foundational position in the curriculum removes any scaffolding-based protection. The rating stays High, hedged by real ten-year uncertainty about adoption pace in health care specifically, an industry the evidence palette flags as slower-diffusing than technology-forward sectors despite the underlying capability being available.
HCM 4300.d: This course is designed to discuss the role of the health care manager in health care planning and strategic management, as well as the concepts and methodology of strategic management as applied in health care. Emphasis is placed on how health care organizations adapt in a rapidly changing environment.

r: This course synthesizes health care management and computer information systems content, covering administrative systems, clinical decision support, health information exchange, and digital imaging applications that interface with the electronic medical record, plus case studies of the data flows and business processes each supports. The work is Interacting With Computers and Analyzing Data or Information almost entirely, with no clinical or physical presence required, so F3 is fully digital. Task-exposure research finds programming- and analysis-adjacent tasks strongly positively associated with AI exposure, and current usage data shows this category already dominant. AI can already explain interfaces, summarize case studies, and map data flows competently. Verification still matters because health-IT errors touch protected data and clinical workflows, keeping F2 moderate rather than negligible. No licensure gate applies, so the 24-month rating sits at Medium, reflecting strong but not yet complete exposure.

By 2031, AI should competently explain and troubleshoot the interfaces among EMR-adjacent systems, clinical decision support, health information exchange, and imaging applications that this course surveys, consistent with productivity research showing large gains on structured technical-writing and analysis tasks and with enterprise API usage skewing toward automation rather than augmentation. The course's synthesis-and-case-study format is precisely the kind of applied knowledge transfer AI performs well when verified. Some verification burden persists because health-IT decisions touch protected health information and downstream clinical safety, but this is a narrower constraint than outright licensure. No accreditation or embodiment barrier holds the rating down, and the fully digital, non-foundational character of the course places it among the more exposed courses in the batch. The rating moves to High, tracking the general trajectory of applied information-systems coursework once execution work is largely AI-performable.

Over a longer horizon, capability-trend evidence on expanding AI task-time horizons and continuing compute growth points toward AI handling most routine analysis of health information system interfaces, data flows, and compliance considerations that this course teaches, and diffusion into health-IT administrative functions should be considerably more mature than the current uneven base rate. The applied knowledge-synthesis work central to the course is highly automatable in a central-case reading. What is genuinely uncertain is how much decision-making authority over clinical-adjacent data systems organizations keep vested in trained human analysts given persistent privacy and safety verification needs; that uncertainty argues for hedging rather than treating the course as maximally exposed. With no licensure lock and a terminal position in the curriculum, the rating holds at High, acknowledging real but bounded residual verification demands in a regulated health-data environment.
HCM 4350.d: This course presents a synthesis of health care management (HCM) and computer information systems (CIS) content to prepare the student for decision-making responsibilities as a practitioner in the field of health care information systems. A review of critical concepts from the HCM and CIS curriculum for the B.S. in Health Care Information Systems curriculum will be followed by an overview of applications used in the health care industry that interact with and support the electronic medical record (covered in HCM 4150), including administrative systems, clinical decision support, health information exchange, and digital clinical imaging applications. Discussion of these applications will include a review of data gathered by each, the interfaces sharing data with other applications, the business and clinical processes supported by each, and a case study that synthesizes the relationships among health information applications.

r: HCM 4500 has students prepare a resume, build informational-interviewing skill, secure a practicum placement agency and preceptor, and draft a practicum project proposal. The resume and proposal-writing tasks map to Documenting/Recording Information, a strongly AI-exposed writing category where drafting assistance is already common and effective. But the course's binding role is structural, not content-based: it is the mandatory gateway MSU Denver requires the semester before HCM 4510, the Health Care Management Practicum, making it critical scaffolding that many students' capstone placement depends on. That foundational role caps the rating regardless of how automatable resume drafting becomes. Informational interviewing and preceptor selection also involve real interpersonal negotiation AI cannot conduct on the student's behalf. At 24 months the rating is Medium: exposed writing tasks pull upward, the prerequisite-gateway role holds it back from High.
